door.cc: I get short of breath when I walk.

cases.persona: A 74-year-old retired school librarian, warm and chatty, who apologizes for 'making a fuss' and blames her age and her weight. She pauses to catch her breath in long answers and sits upright on the edge of the chair. She knows her pills well but admits she forgets them, and she is more worried than she lets on.
cases.opening: I just can't walk like I used to without getting winded. It's been creeping up on me for months.

It's not a pain, dear, it's my breathing. There's nothing to point to.

I'm up to three pillows now. I used to sleep on one. Some nights I end up in the recliner, because lying flat makes me feel like I'm drowning.

I've put on about eight pounds in the last two months, and I'm eating less, so it doesn't make sense to me.

A little dry tickle of a cough at night when I lie down. Nothing comes up.
No, no chest pain at all.
No vomiting and no sweats. My appetite is down a bit, and I feel full quickly.
No fevers or chills. I'm tired all the time now. And the weight gain, like I said.
No blood. No wheezing that I can hear.
No heartburn. No real belly pain, just that full feeling.
No weakness on one side, no trouble speaking, no vision changes. My mind's still sharp.
No, I think that's everything. It's mostly the breathing and the swelling.
High blood pressure for about twenty-five years, type 2 diabetes for about ten, and arthritis in my knees.
No heart attacks, no stents. I had a stress test three years ago and they told me there were no blockages.
My gallbladder out in 1998, and both cataracts done a few years ago.
Only for the gallbladder, and having my two children.
Amlodipine 10 milligrams every morning for my blood pressure, for about three years. Metformin 1,000 milligrams twice a day for about ten years. Atorvastatin 20 milligrams at night for about five.
Honestly, I forget the blood pressure pill maybe twice a week.

A glass of wine at Thanksgiving and Christmas. That's all.

I used to walk the neighborhood every morning. I've had to stop.

My father had a stroke at 76.

exam.position: She lies back with the head of the bed at 30 degrees and says she could not lie any flatter.
exam.general-survey: Alert and oriented, sitting upright, mildly short of breath after walking into the room but speaking in full sentences. Normal color, no sweating, no distress at rest.
exam.jvp: Jugular venous distention at 30 degrees, with the pulsation visible about 5 centimeters above the sternal angle.
exam.precordium-palp: A sustained lift at the apex (mitral area). No heaves or lifts over the other areas.
exam.pmi: The point of maximal impulse is forceful and sustained, about 3 centimeters across, at the fifth intercostal space in the left midclavicular line. It is not displaced.
exam.ausc-mitral: Mitral area: regular rhythm, normal first and second heart sounds, with a soft, dull extra sound just before the first heart sound (a fourth heart sound). No murmur.
exam.left-lateral: Left lateral decubitus, bell at the apex: a dull, low-pitched fourth heart sound just before the first heart sound, the 'Ten-nes-SEE' cadence. No third heart sound, no murmur.
exam.ext-inspect: Both lower legs are symmetrically swollen from the feet to mid-shin, with deep sock-line marks. No brown staining, no varicose veins, no ulcers; normal hair growth.
exam.edema: 2+ pitting edema, symmetric, over the dorsum of both feet, behind the medial malleoli and up the shins to mid-shin.
exam.bp-both-arms: Right arm 162/88 mmHg, left arm 158/86 mmHg: within 10 mmHg between the arms, high on both.

special: presses firmly over the right upper abdomen for about 10 seconds while watching the neck veins
Positive: the jugular venous pulsation rises and stays up for as long as the pressure is held.
palpates upward from the right lower abdomen for the liver edge below the right costal margin
The liver edge is smooth and slightly tender, palpable about 2 centimeters below the right costal margin.

key.diagnosis: Chronic heart failure, most likely with preserved ejection fraction from long-standing hypertension (New York Heart Association class III, with fluid overload but stable for outpatient care)
must_not_miss: Acute decompensated heart failure: breathlessness at rest, chest pain or fainting means the emergency department now
Acute coronary syndrome as a hidden trigger: a troponin if there is any concern for a heart attack

ddx.name: Chronic heart failure (most likely preserved ejection fraction)
ddx.support: Exertional breathlessness now at 50 yards, three-pillow orthopnea, waking up gasping, bilateral pitting edema, rings tight, 8-pound weight gain, early fullness, raised neck veins, a positive hepatojugular reflux and an enlarged liver. High blood pressure with a sustained, nondisplaced apical impulse and a fourth heart sound points to a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle with a preserved ejection fraction.
ddx.against: Clear lungs; crackles are often absent in chronic failure even with fluid overload, and the echocardiogram still has to set the ejection fraction group.

ddx.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
ddx.support: Forty pack-years of smoking, exertional breathlessness and a night-time cough.
ddx.against: No wheeze and nothing coughed up; orthopnea, waking up gasping, raised neck veins and a fourth heart sound point to the heart, and a high natriuretic peptide points away.

ddx.name: Chronic venous insufficiency
ddx.support: Ankle swelling that is worse by evening and better in the morning.
ddx.against: Both legs equally, with breathlessness and raised neck veins; no brown staining, varicose veins or ulcers.

ddx.name: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker edema
ddx.support: She takes amlodipine, which causes dependent ankle swelling.
ddx.against: Amlodipine started three years before the swelling; raised neck veins, orthopnea and breathlessness are not drug edema.

studies.why: Confirms heart failure as the cause of the breathlessness: above 400 makes it likely, below 100 rules out acute failure.
studies.expect: Elevated, about 640.

studies.why: Measures the ejection fraction, which sets the treatment group: 40% or less reduced, 41 to 49% mildly reduced, 50% or more preserved.
studies.expect: Thick left ventricular walls (hypertrophy), normal chamber size, ejection fraction about 60%: preserved.

studies.why: Looks for congestion (cephalization, Kerley B lines, effusion) and heart size.
studies.expect: Cephalization of the upper lung vessels; no infiltrate.

studies.why: Looks for ischemic changes or left ventricular hypertrophy.
studies.expect: Sinus rhythm at 88 with left ventricular hypertrophy (tall R waves in V5 and V6, deep S waves in V1 and V2); no ischemic changes.

studies.test: Metabolic panel and complete blood count
studies.why: Potassium and kidney function before and during treatment; anemia as a high-output cause of failure.
studies.expect: Potassium and kidney function normal; no anemia.

plan: Preserved ejection fraction: a loop diuretic (furosemide) as needed for the fluid, and a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin) first.

Stop amlodipine (calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure) and control her blood pressure with medicines that suit her other conditions: a renin-angiotensin system blocker (lisinopril or losartan), a beta blocker or spironolactone.
Stop naproxen: anti-inflammatory painkillers hold salt and water.
Follow potassium and kidney function, co-manage with cardiology, and refer to cardiac rehabilitation.
Same-day review if her weight or breathlessness climbs; emergency department for breathlessness at rest, chest pain or fainting.
education: Your heart muscle has grown thick and stiff from years of high blood pressure, so it cannot fill well, and fluid backs up into your lungs and legs. That is why lying flat makes you breathless and your ankles swell.
Weigh yourself every morning. Call for a gain of more than 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 in a week: an overnight gain is fluid, not fat.
Take every medicine every day, even when you feel well; the goals are a longer life and slower progression, not just comfort.
Limit salt, stop the naproxen and other anti-inflammatory painkillers, stay off cigarettes, keep alcohol low.
Call the same day for more pillows, waking up gasping, swelling climbing your legs, less urine or new confusion; call 911 for breathlessness at rest, chest pain or fainting.
key.follow_up: Routine: clinic follow-up with cardiology co-management to start and adjust therapy and to recheck potassium and kidney function; same-day review if her weight or breathlessness climbs.
key.presentation: Mrs. Whitcomb is a 74-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension, type 2 diabetes and a 40 pack-year former smoking history, presenting with four months of worsening exertional breathlessness, now after 50 yards. She sleeps on three pillows, up from one, wakes gasping once or twice a week, and has evening ankle swelling with an eight-pound weight gain. She takes amlodipine and daily naproxen. She denies chest pain, palpitations, fainting, wheeze and productive cough. Blood pressure is 162/88, heart rate 88, saturation 95%. Examination shows jugular venous distention, a positive hepatojugular reflux, an enlarged liver, a sustained, nondisplaced apical impulse, a fourth heart sound, clear lungs and 2+ pitting edema to mid-shin. My differential is chronic heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, venous insufficiency and amlodipine edema. I would order a natriuretic peptide, echocardiogram, chest X-ray, electrocardiogram and metabolic panel. My working diagnosis is chronic heart failure, likely preserved ejection fraction. Plan: a diuretic and a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor, stop amlodipine and naproxen, daily weights, cardiology.

high_yield.item: Ask how many pillows she sleeps on, and why
high_yield.why: Quantifies orthopnea: one pillow a year ago, three now, sometimes the recliner.

high_yield.item: Ask whether she wakes up at night gasping
high_yield.why: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, an hour or two after lying down, is a heart failure symptom; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease does not give it.

high_yield.item: Measure the jugular venous pressure at 30 to 45 degrees, then do the hepatojugular reflux
high_yield.why: Raised neck veins separate heart failure from venous insufficiency and drug edema.

high_yield.item: Locate and size the apical impulse; listen with the bell at the apex in left lateral decubitus
high_yield.why: A sustained, nondisplaced impulse with a fourth heart sound means a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle (preserved ejection fraction); a displaced, diffuse one with a third heart sound means a dilated ventricle.

high_yield.item: Grade the pitting edema and say how high it climbs
high_yield.why: Thumb for 2 seconds over the foot, behind the medial malleolus and on the shin; symmetric 2+ to mid-shin.

high_yield.item: Ask about over-the-counter medicines
high_yield.why: Daily naproxen holds salt and water; amlodipine is also a cause of ankle swelling and is avoided in heart failure.

high_yield.item: Listen to the lung bases and say what clear lungs mean
high_yield.why: Clear lungs do not exclude heart failure: crackles are often absent in chronic failure even with fluid overload, and finding them would point to decompensation.

high_yield.item: Teach daily weights with numbers
high_yield.why: More than 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 in a week is fluid and needs a call.

door.name: Marjorie Pell
door.setting: Outpatient primary care clinic, same-day visit
door.cc: My heart has been acting funny since last night.

cases.persona: A 76-year-old retired bank teller, brisk and talkative, a little rattled, who keeps pressing her palm to her chest while she talks. She is precise about dates and times and jumps to the worst case because of what happened to her mother. She settles down when things are explained plainly.
cases.opening: Since last night my heart's been doing something strange, and it hasn't stopped. It has me rattled.
facts: Last night around nine. We'd just come home from my granddaughter's engagement dinner and I was sitting on the couch when it started, all of a sudden.
(Presses her palm flat over the left side of her chest.) In here. It's not a pain, it's the beating.
It hasn't stopped once since last night. So about fifteen hours now.
Racing and fluttering, all over the place. There's no steady beat to it, like a drummer who can't keep time.
Irregular. Completely irregular, not just fast.
Nothing has helped. I tried lying down, deep breaths, a glass of cold water.
Walking around makes me more winded. The stairs this morning were hard.
It doesn't go anywhere. There's no pain to go anywhere.
Maybe a four out of ten. It's more frightening than painful. A ten was giving birth to my son.
Constant since it started. It's the same now as it was at midnight.
Once, maybe six months ago, I had a few minutes of fluttering after my morning coffee, and it stopped by itself. I didn't tell anyone.
No chest pain. Just the fluttering.
I got winded walking up the stairs this morning, which isn't like me. Sitting still I'm all right.
One pillow, as always. I lay flat last night trying to sleep and my breathing was fine.
Waking at night short of breath

key.diagnosis: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, hemodynamically stable, first documented episode about 15 hours ago (one brief self-limited episode six months ago)

Unstable atrial fibrillation (hypotension, pulmonary edema or an acute myocardial infarction), which needs synchronized cardioversion

ddx.name: Atrial fibrillation

ddx.against: Seen in acutely ill lung or heart failure patients; she has neither, and the electrocardiogram would show a P wave of at least three shapes before every beat.

studies.why: Confirms the rhythm and separates it from flutter, multifocal atrial tachycardia and premature atrial contractions.
studies.expect: Irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm at about 124, no P waves and no PR interval.

studies.why: Stroke risk, which decides anticoagulation; 0 in a man or 1 in a woman is low risk.
studies.expect: 4 (female, age 75 or older, high blood pressure): high risk, so she needs anticoagulation.

studies.why: Bleeding risk on anticoagulation.

studies.expect: Normal.

plan: She is stable (normal blood pressure, no pulmonary edema, no chest pain) but has a rapid ventricular response: intravenous rate control (diltiazem or metoprolol) in the emergency department today.
Then oral rate control, a beta blocker (metoprolol) or a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil); rate, not rhythm, is goal one.

Anticoagulate for a CHA2DS2-VASc of 4: a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban or dabigatran) for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, or warfarin to an international normalized ratio of 2 to 3.

Risk factors: cut alcohol, lose weight, test for and treat sleep apnea, keep blood pressure controlled.

key.follow_up: Same day: the emergency department today for intravenous rate control and the anticoagulation decision, then cardiology follow-up, with outpatient cardioversion only after 21 days of anticoagulation.
key.presentation: Mrs. Pell is a 76-year-old woman with hypertension presenting with about 15 hours of a racing, fluttering, irregular heartbeat that began suddenly last night after more wine than usual. I would order an electrocardiogram, thyroid-stimulating hormone, electrolytes and an echocardiogram; CHA2DS2-VASc is 4. door.name: Walter Ostrowski
door.cc: I almost passed out on the stairs last week.

cases.persona: A 79-year-old retired machinist, polite, slow-spoken and stoic, who hates a fuss. He answers only what he is asked and needs a direct question before he admits the chest tightness he has been ignoring. His wife made the appointment and he keeps saying it was probably nothing.
cases.opening: Last week I was climbing the stairs at my daughter's and everything went gray. I had to sit down.
facts: A week ago Sunday, climbing the stairs at my daughter's house with a bag of groceries. About two-thirds of the way up, everything went gray and my legs went weak.
I grabbed the rail and sat down on the step. I didn't black out completely. In about a minute it cleared, and I was myself again, no confusion.
No racing heart, no flutter, no warning like that. I was just working hard on the stairs.
Not the graying out. That was the first time.
Since you ask, yes. For about two months I get a tightness in my chest when I walk more than a block or two, or do stairs.
(Rubs the middle of his chest with an open hand.) Across the middle here.
A few minutes. It goes once I stop and rest.
Tight, like a band across my chest. Not sharp.
Walking any distance, stairs, carrying things, working in the garden.
No, lying down or taking a deep breath doesn't change it.
A four out of ten, maybe. A ten was crushing my thumb in a lathe back in 1982.
Only when I exert myself. Never sitting still, never at night. About the same over these two months.
Yes, I get out of breath walking any distance now, along with the tightness. Sitting here I'm fine.
One pillow. I can lie flat fine.
Waking at night short of breath
No, my heart doesn't race or skip.
No, my legs are fine. It's the chest and the wind that stop me.
No fevers. I tire out more than I used to. My weight's steady.
No weakness on one side, no trouble talking, no vision changes. When I grayed out it was everything at once, not one side.
Now that you mention it, a doctor told me about five years ago that I had a murmur. He said to keep an eye on it. Nobody ever did anything about it.
High blood pressure and high cholesterol, both for about fifteen years. A bit of arthritis in my hands.
A hernia repair in 1995 and a prostate procedure in 2016. Never had a heart test that I know of, other than the heart tracing at physicals.
One night after the prostate procedure. That's all.
Rheumatic fever, childhood heart problem or kidney disease
No, none that I know of.
Lisinopril 20 milligrams in the morning and atorvastatin 40 milligrams at night. Both for years.
A baby aspirin some days, fish oil, and Tylenol for my hands.
About a pack a day from eighteen until I was fifty, so about thirty years. I quit in 1997.
A beer or two on bowling night.
I don't drink much water. Coffee in the morning, and the beer on bowling night.
Retired machinist. Forty years in a machine shop, around cutting oils and metal dust, but my lungs have always been fine.
Gardening, and bowling on Thursdays. I've sat out bowling the last month because I get winded carrying the ball bag.
My wife cooks. Meat and potatoes, mostly.
I live with my wife, Irene, in a one-story house. Our daughter lives across town; that's the house with the stairs.
Yes, on the lisinopril. They say it's under control.
My father died of a stroke at 77.

My brother had bypass surgery at 72. My sister is fine.

I figured I went up the stairs too fast. Old age.
Irene's worried it'll happen when I'm driving. I suppose I'd like to know what's going on.
questions: Is there a pill for this, or do I need an operation?
Can I keep bowling and working in the garden?

exam.carotid-inspect: Carotid pulsations are small and slow to rise on both sides.
exam.carotid-ausc: A harsh systolic sound over both carotids, loudest low in the neck, that can be followed continuously down to the right second intercostal space.
exam.carotid-palp: Carotid upstrokes are weak and delayed on both sides: slow to rise and low in volume. No thrill.
exam.precordium-palp: A forceful, sustained lift at the apex (mitral area). No heaves or lifts over the other areas.
exam.pmi: The point of maximal impulse is forceful and sustained, a little over 2 centimeters across, at the fifth intercostal space in the left midclavicular line. It is not displaced.
exam.thrills: A thrill is felt with the ball of the hand over the aortic area, second intercostal space at the right sternal border. No thrills elsewhere.
exam.ausc-aortic: Aortic area: a harsh, medium-pitched, midsystolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur, grade 4 out of 6, loudest here and radiating to both carotids. Regular rhythm at about 72. No diastolic murmur.
exam.ausc-pulmonic: Pulmonic area: the same systolic murmur, softer, carried over from the aortic area.
exam.ausc-erb: Erb's point: the systolic murmur is heard more softly down the left sternal border.
exam.ausc-tricuspid: Tricuspid area: the systolic murmur is faint here.
exam.ausc-mitral: Mitral area: the systolic murmur is faint at the apex. A soft fourth heart sound just before the first heart sound.
exam.left-lateral: Left lateral decubitus, bell at the apex: a dull, low-pitched fourth heart sound just before the first heart sound. No third heart sound; the systolic murmur is faint here.
exam.lean-forward: Sitting up and leaning forward at end-expiration: the harsh systolic murmur is louder at the right upper sternal border. No diastolic murmur and no rub.
exam.dynamic: Squatting from standing, or a passive leg raise: the murmur gets louder. Valsalva or standing quickly: it gets softer. Isometric handgrip: softer.
exam.bp-both-arms: Right arm 126/84 mmHg, left arm 124/84 mmHg: within 10 mmHg between the arms.

special: places one hand on the apical impulse and the other on the right carotid at the same time
A forceful, sustained apical impulse, while the carotid upstroke under the other hand is weak and arrives late.
keeps a finger on the carotid while listening at the aortic area
The murmur coincides with the carotid upstroke: it is systolic.

key.diagnosis: Symptomatic aortic stenosis, likely severe and degenerative (calcific) in a man over 70
must_not_miss: Coronary artery disease causing the exertional chest tightness: the two often coexist, so the murmur does not end the angina workup
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy: exertional near-fainting with a systolic murmur

ddx.name: Aortic stenosis
ddx.support: Exertional chest tightness, breathlessness and near-fainting on the stairs in a 79-year-old man with a murmur known for five years; a harsh grade 4 out of 6 midsystolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the right second intercostal space with a thrill, radiating to both carotids, louder with squatting and leaning forward, softer with Valsalva and handgrip; a forceful, sustained apex with a weak, delayed carotid; a fourth heart sound.
ddx.against: Nothing; the echocardiogram grades the severity.

ddx.name: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
ddx.support: Exertional near-fainting with a systolic murmur.
ddx.against: Age 79 with no family history of sudden death; the murmur is loudest at the right second intercostal space and carries into the carotids, not at Erb's point; it gets softer, not louder, with Valsalva and standing.

ddx.name: Mitral regurgitation
ddx.support: A systolic murmur with exertional breathlessness.
ddx.against: Midsystolic and loudest at the base, carrying into the neck, not holosystolic at the apex into the axilla; softer, not louder, with handgrip.

ddx.name: Stable angina from coronary artery disease
ddx.support: Exertional chest tightness relieved by rest in an older former smoker with high blood pressure and high cholesterol.
ddx.against: The ejection murmur, the carotid findings and the near-fainting point to the valve, but the two often coexist.

studies.why: Confirms and grades the stenosis, and excludes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and mitral regurgitation; anyone with symptoms suggestive of aortic stenosis gets one.
studies.expect: Thickened, calcified aortic leaflets with reduced systolic opening and left ventricular hypertrophy; valve area 0.8 square centimeters, mean gradient 48 mmHg, jet velocity 4.3 meters per second: severe (the '4, 40 and 1' rule). Normal septum, no regurgitant mitral jet.

studies.why: Left ventricular hypertrophy in severe disease (low sensitivity).
studies.expect: Sinus rhythm at 72 with left ventricular hypertrophy.

studies.why: The definitive finding.
studies.expect: Confirms a severe gradient across the aortic valve.

plan: Urgent cardiology valve referral: every patient with aortic stenosis on echocardiogram goes to cardiology.
Severe and symptomatic: aortic valve replacement, by transcatheter aortic valve replacement or with a mechanical valve (lifelong anticoagulation) or a biological valve.
No medicine fixes the valve, and he is preload dependent: avoid dehydration, strenuous activity and competitive sports.
Avoid nitrates for the chest tightness, and keep beta blockers and calcium channel blockers out of his blood pressure regimen.
education: The valve out of your heart has narrowed, so your heart has to work harder to push blood through it. When it cannot keep up during effort, you get the chest tightness, the breathlessness and the graying out.
Now that it causes symptoms, the plan is to replace the valve, so the heart specialist needs to see you soon.
Drink enough fluids, avoid heavy exertion, and do not take nitroglycerin unless the heart specialist prescribes it.
Report chest pain, fainting or breathlessness on exertion right away; they change the plan.
Keep the echocardiogram and the cardiology appointments.
red_flags: Chest pain that does not settle with rest
Breathlessness at rest or lying flat, or waking up gasping
key.follow_up: Urgent: echocardiogram and cardiology valve referral within days, because he has symptoms.
key.presentation: Mr. Ostrowski is a 79-year-old man with hypertension, high cholesterol, former smoking and a murmur noted five years ago, presenting after nearly fainting on the stairs last week. He also has two months of exertional chest tightness and breathlessness after a block or two, relieved by rest. He denies palpitations, rest pain, orthopnea, leg swelling and family sudden death. Vital signs are normal. He has a harsh grade 4 out of 6 midsystolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the right second intercostal space with a thrill, radiating to both carotids, louder with squatting and leaning forward, softer with Valsalva and handgrip; a forceful, sustained apical impulse with weak, delayed carotid upstrokes; a fourth heart sound; and clear lungs. My differential is aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, mitral regurgitation and coronary artery disease. I would order an echocardiogram and electrocardiogram, then left heart catheterization. My working diagnosis is symptomatic, likely severe aortic stenosis. Plan: urgent cardiology for valve replacement, no nitrates, and no dehydration or strenuous exertion.

high_yield.why: The three cardinal symptoms; once any appears, 3-year mortality is 75% without valve replacement.

high_yield.item: Describe the murmur completely: timing, location, radiation, grade, quality
high_yield.why: Timing first (palpate the carotid while listening); harsh, midsystolic, right second intercostal space, into both carotids.

high_yield.item: Feel for a thrill over the aortic area
high_yield.why: A thrill means grade 4 out of 6 or more.

high_yield.item: Trace the sound from the aortic area into both carotids before calling it a bruit

high_yield.why: No nitrates, avoid dehydration and strenuous exertion, urgent echocardiogram and cardiology.

door.name: Teresa Vandermolen

Standing at the chair all day, and sitting a long time with my feet down, like on a long drive.
No, it stays in the lower legs.

One pillow. I lie flat fine.
Waking at night short of breath
No fevers, no weight change. Tired at the end of a long day, like anyone.
Nothing unusual with my urine. No one has ever said I have a kidney or liver problem.
No numbness or weakness. My feet feel normal.
No, it's just the legs. And the sore.
High blood pressure for about six years, and I'm heavier than I'd like.
Yes, a blood clot in my left leg when I was 48, after my hysterectomy. I was on a blood thinner for three months.
No cancer, no long trips or time off my feet lately, and no clotting problems in the family.
I've never worn compression stockings. No leg ulcers or skin infections before this.
The hysterectomy in 2013 for fibroids. No vein procedures.
The hysterectomy, and the blood clot afterward. And three deliveries.
Lisinopril 10 milligrams in the morning for about six years. No blood thinners now.
Tylenol now and then for my back, and a multivitamin.
I smoked in my twenties, maybe half a pack a day, and quit at thirty.
A glass of wine on the weekend.
I've been a hairstylist for thirty-five years. On my feet at the chair all day, nine or ten hours.
Not much besides work. I'm too tired after.
I live with my husband, Ray. Our kids are grown.
Yes, on the lisinopril. It runs fine.
My mother had terrible varicose veins and sores on her legs that took forever to heal. She lived to 84.
My father had high blood pressure and died of a heart attack at 79.
My sister has varicose veins too.
My mother's legs. I always knew they'd catch up with me.

exam.ext-inspect: Brown discoloration around both ankles, worse on the left, starting at the inner ankle bone, with dry, scaly, red skin and shiny, taut skin. A shallow 2-centimeter ulcer just above the left inner ankle bone with irregular borders, a clean yellowish base and a little clear drainage; no surrounding redness. Normal hair growth.
exam.edema: 2+ pitting edema over the left ankle and lower shin, 1+ over the right ankle, stopping well below the knees.
exam.bp-both-arms: Right arm 128/78 mmHg, left arm 126/78 mmHg: within 10 mmHg between the arms.

special: has the patient stand and inspects both legs from the groin to the feet, front and back

Standing: dilated, tortuous superficial veins along the inner thigh and calf of both legs, more on the left, visible and palpable and mildly tender. The swelling and the color change look more obvious.
feels both legs with the back of the hand, then palpates along the deep veins of each calf
Both legs are the same normal temperature, with no heat. No tenderness along the deep veins; the calves are soft.
measures both calves 10 centimeters below the tibial tuberosity

key.diagnosis: Chronic venous insufficiency (secondary, after her left leg deep vein thrombosis) with varicose veins, stasis dermatitis and a venous ulcer above the left medial malleolus
must_not_miss: Deep vein thrombosis: new one-sided swelling with calf pain and warmth; the venous duplex ultrasound settles it
Peripheral artery disease: an arterial ulcer, weak pulses or a low ankle-brachial index means no compression

ddx.name: Chronic venous insufficiency and varicose veins
ddx.support: Years of heavy, aching legs worse with standing and better with elevation and walking; evening ankle swelling; itching and brown staining starting at the left medial malleolus; a weeping ulcer above it; varicose veins on standing. Risk factors: prior left leg clot, female, age, three pregnancies, obesity, decades of standing at work, and a mother and sister with varicose veins.
ddx.against: Nothing; the duplex scan confirms reflux and excludes a clot.

ddx.name: Peripheral artery disease
ddx.support: A leg ulcer in a woman over 60 with high blood pressure and a smoking history.
ddx.against: No pain with walking (walking helps); warm legs with normal hair, normal pulses and capillary refill; the ulcer sits above the medial malleolus with a clean base, not on the toes or lateral ankle; edema is present.

ddx.name: Deep vein thrombosis
ddx.support: A prior left leg clot, and the left leg is more swollen.
ddx.against: Years of slow symptoms rather than acute swelling over days; no new calf pain, heat or deep-vein tenderness; calves differ by only 1 centimeter.

ddx.name: Heart failure, kidney or liver disease
ddx.support: Swelling in both ankles.
ddx.against: Asymmetric, with varicose veins, staining and an ulcer; normal neck veins, clear lungs, no breathlessness or orthopnea, and no kidney or liver history; she takes no calcium channel blocker or anti-inflammatory painkiller.

studies.why: The first test: confirms the diagnosis, checks patency (is there a clot?) and valve competence (is there reflux?), and maps the reflux.
studies.expect: Valvular reflux in the great saphenous vein on both sides and scarred, incompetent deep valves in the left leg from the old clot; the deep veins are patent and compressible, with no thrombus.

studies.why: Rules out arterial disease before compression, and is done for any lower leg wound.
studies.expect: 1.05 on both sides: normal, so compression is safe.

studies.why: The gold standard, but kept for planning an intervention.
studies.expect: Not needed now.

plan: Nonoperative first: elevate the legs above heart level, daily walking and ankle flexion, avoid long spells of sitting or standing, gentle cleansing and emollients.
